title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
text:
What is genomic variation?
Most of a person’s genome is the same as another person’s. All humans need the same proteins to function. But very small parts of our genome, especially in the areas that do not code for proteins, can vary across individuals. This genomic variation is caused by changes in the nucleotide sequences that can cause differences in how a protein functions or the amount of protein created. Some variations can change the function of a protein so severely that it stops doing its intended function, while others can increase or decrease the amount of protein that is produced.
These variations in a genome are caused by mutations. Mutations are any changes in the DNA or nucleotides that make up the genome.

Mutation is just a term for any change to the DNA. Not all mutations are deleterious or bad. Many have no impact at all and some can be beneficial.

These variations can be caused by a change of a single nucleotide (“point mutations”) or changes involving more than one nucleotide. An example of a single nucleotide change would be changing a base from C → T or adding or removing a single nucleotide (pronounced “snip”).









If a point mutation occurs fairly often within a population and is observed with a common frequency, it is termed a single-nucleotide polymorphism or SNP (pronounced “snip”).
Sometimes mutations involve more than one nucleotide. An example of a mutation involving more than one nucleotide would be if a chunk of DNA, like ACCGT, were to be repeated and become ACCGTACCGT (such changes with more than 50 nucleotides are called structural variants). Some large structural changes (like the Translocation shown in the figure below) may even occur across multiple chromosomes (inter-chromosomal) rather than being within a single chromosome (intra-chromosomal).

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
text:
How do nucleotide changes happen?
Variation can be introduced into the genome through mutation or recombination during meiosis. Mutations may occur due to errors during the replication of genomic material during cell division, imperfect repair mechanisms not catching mistakes, environmental factors or mutagens that damage genomic material (e.g., high-energy radiation or certain chemicals or viruses), or spontaneous/random changes.


Mutations


Changes to the DNA that can either be a single nucleotide change, larger changes involving segments of nucleotides, or in some cases changes to other chemical modifications of the DNA that change how tightly it is wound. See this article for more information.


No matter the cause of mutation, not all variations will be passed on to offspring/children. Mutations may be somatic (occurring in cells that are not part of the reproductive system) or germline (occurring in cells that are part of the reproductive system). Germline mutations and meiotic recombination are examples of heritable variation that will be passed on to future generations.



Human genomes are large (over 3 billion nucleotide base pairs)! And most of the genome is identical when comparing two individuals or an individual to a reference genome. On average, if you compared the genomes of two individuals, there would be >99% matching between the two. This is often visualized with a dotplot where highly identical genomes will have a dense, diagonal line with some off-diagonal dots (or lines for larger variants like an insertion or duplication).













More details about dotplots

Besides comparing two human samples to each other, dotplots are also used to compare a human sample to a reference genome, reference genomes to each other, human samples or reference genomes to other species, or really any other species/sample comparison.
Comparisons for less related samples produce more complex dotplots that represent larger structural variants like the inversions in the following example.

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
section: Why should we care about human genomic variation?
text:
Why should we care about human genomic variation?
Especially if there’s so much similarity, why should we care about human genomic variation? Not all variations or mutations have an impact. Some variations can be “functional” and lead to changes not just in the genome, but also in the proteins that are translated from the genetic material. However, not all variation is “functional”; some changes don’t impact the proteins that are translated from the genetic material. (See silent mutations below).
Functional changes, on the other hand, may impact how much of a protein is made, the protein structure, and therefore its eventual role in the cell, or where and when the protein is expressed due to changes in parts of the genome that help regulate gene transcription. Certain diseases may be caused or worsened by genetic variation. Cancer is a common example of this, where genes that control cell growth, division, or scheduled cell death are mutated, and their proteins do not function properly to control the cell cycle, leading to uncontrolled cell growth that develops into tumors.
For other diseases, a protein may not be expressed at the correct levels or the protein may be folded incorrectly because of its mutated structure, leading to inefficiencies in or the inability of the protein to perform its function(s). This is the case in the mutation that leads to sickle-cell anemia and changes in the hemoglobin protein. To protect against this, there are biological redundancies that act as a safety net. These create backup systems that can mitigate issues by compensating for or taking the place of nonfunctional components. But even with redundancies and safety nets, mutations can lead to small changes with major consequences.




Different types of (single-nucleotide) mutations

As mentioned earlier, there are a few different types of mutations. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms are single-base pair differences, while larger structural mutations change more than one nucleotide. Within the group of single-nucleotide mutations, there are different types that are defined based on the effect of the mutation.

SummaryComparisonSilentMissenseNonsenseFrameshift


Single-nucleotide changes
Different types of single-nucleotide mutations are defined based on the effect of the mutation.

Silent mutations have an underlying nucleotide change, but the amino acid building blocks of the protein remain unchanged. Not only does the protein remain unchanged, but for a true “silent” mutation, there is no effect on the cell.
Synonymous mutations: Synonymous mutations have an underlying nucleotide change, and the amino acid building blocks of the protein remain unchanged. They differ from silent mutations, however, because these have an impact on the cell.
Missense mutations result in an amino acid substitution, which can impact protein structure and function.

Some missense mutations are “conservative” where the amino acid substitution is switching one amino acid for another similar one with similar biochemical properties (e.g., size, charge, etc.).
A “non-conservative” missense mutation switches an amino acid to one with dissimilar biochemical properties – this is likely to have a greater impact on protein structure and function than a conservative missense mutation.

Nonsense mutations introduce an early stop codon, halting translation and producing a truncated, likely nonfunctional protein.

Single-nucleotide insertions or deletions (indels)
A single nucleotide insertion or deletion (AKA an “indel”) may introduce a frameshift mutation. Frameshift mutations often impact the structure and function of proteins because of the shifting of the reading frame during translation for all subsequent codons after the insertion or deletion.

Silent mutations have an underlying base pair change (i.e., a C to an A), but the amino acid building blocks of the protein remain unchanged. Since these mutations do not change the encoded amino acid, they are called silent. However, these silent mutations may still impact how often a protein is produced because certain tRNA anticodons are less available or may take longer to process in translation; so while they code for the same amino acid, they may not be truly “silent” and may have an effect in the cell. Such mutations are called synonymous mutations.


Missense mutations result in an amino acid substitution, which can impact protein structure and function. The single nucleotide change altered the amino acid that was encoded by that segment of DNA. This causes a substitution in the amino acid encoded for in that part of the protein. Some missense mutations are “conservative” where the amino acid substitution is switching one amino acid for another similar one with similar biochemical properties (e.g., size, charge, etc.). A “non-conservative” missense mutation switches an amino acid to one with dissimilar biochemical properties - this is likely to have a greater impact on protein structure and function than a conservative missense mutation.



Nonsense mutations introduce an early stop codon - halting translation prematurely. A stop codon typically signals the end of a segment of RNA that encodes a protein, signaling the end of translation. An early stop codon will prematurely stop the production of the protein and result in a shorter (or truncated), often non-functional protein.



A single nucleotide insertion or deletion (also known as an “indel”), or an insertion or deletion that is a length not a multiple of three (which is the length of a codon), may introduce a frameshift mutation. Frameshift mutations often impact structure and function to a higher degree than missense mutations because these cause downstream impacts, shifting the reading frame during translation for all subsequent RNA codons. When genetic material is read to create a protein, it is read in three-nucleotide chunks – the reading frame. A shift in the reading frame can greatly impact how a protein is made.

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
section: Why do genetic changes sometimes persist in populations?
text:
Why do genetic changes sometimes persist in populations?
Genetic variation is considered necessary for survival. Scientists hypothesize that species are under various selective pressures to adapt and retain genetic changes that allow them to survive and reproduce, especially when competing with other species (e.g., predators vs prey, virus-host interactions, etc.) Given this, heritable variation (e.g., recombination during meiosis or germline mutations that are passed from generation to generation) can be beneficial by allowing for the selection of advantageous traits for adaptation leading to better survival. In other words, evolution depends upon the random accidents and mistakes that are mutations being maintained within a population because the changes can be advantageous.
Every person alive inherited genomic material from two individuals, and each of those individuals inherited genomic material from two other individuals, continuing backwards through their family history. Each generation of people pass down genomic materials to the next. Since genomic material is what is passed down from ancestors, genomic material is what is compared when considering ancestry and studying how individuals are related. Individuals who are more closely related will share more genomic material in common than those who are more distantly related.
Additionally, the length of time is important because time is needed for genetic variation to accumulate. The longer the amount of time or number of generations between two individuals, the more genetic variation there will be. With more time and more generations between two individuals, the more opportunities there are for genetic variations to occur and accumulate. Ancestry is something that is determined and formed over time and through a process – the process of genetic material being passed down. Therefore ancestry is defined as a “process-based concept” of how someone is related to other individuals in their genealogical history. Ancestry is a biological concept that captures the process of genomic material being passed down from generation to generation. But ancestry can mean many different things. It can capture the closer relationships between individuals and their ancestors, as well as the deeper history of people or species over thousands and tens of thousands of years, as they migrated, mixed, and moved.

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
section: How can we describe or quantify ancestry?
text:
How can we describe or quantify ancestry?
Ancestry captures a process that occurs over time and generations. When talking about ancestry, it can be complicated to quantify it. One way to do this is to compare the genomic material shared between individuals.
When comparing genomic material between individuals, how similar or identical a sequence is between the two is a quantitative measure describing how much overlap or matching there is between the genomic material. Homology is a qualitative description constructed from the amount of similarity and suggests that the sequences or genomic material share a common ancestor. The idea is that if two sequences look similar, they must have come from the same ancestor and diverged relatively recently, since there are few genetic variations that have accumulated. Models used to compare sequences take into account the different kinds of mutations and how commonly they occur.
When thinking about ancestry, we often think about ancestral groups or populations instead of individuals (ex, what group or community an individual is related to or whether one group is related to another group or community). This also applies to studying similarities and differences in current groups based on their ancestry. For example, evaluating every human’s blood pressure on earth would be nearly impossible. It would be much more feasible to study a representative sample of the general population. To create this representative sample, we would need to have individuals who represent different subpopulations within the greater population in our sample or we risk missing important information. Making a representative reference sample is important to make sure the results apply to the general population, and not just the subpopulation that was studied.
To do this, individuals are often grouped based on their ancestry into populations. A population is defined as a group of randomly mating (diploid).Diploid individuals are those with two complete sets of chromosomes (one from each parent) – for example humans. Defining a population is rather subjective. Historically, a lack of migration due to physical boundaries (such as mountains or oceans) influenced population definitions. However, over time, with society overcoming such boundaries, populations that used to be separated have mixed, leading to admixture.


Admixture


Definition of Admixture

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
text:
How do you group humans?
Because of the admixture that has been going on for multiple generations, how populations are partitioned into separate groups is subjective, with no definitive dividing line. An individual’s view of their own ancestry will determine what population they identify as. This adds a cultural, religions, and sometimes geographical element to what used to be a strictly biological concept. People can identify with a culture that is more dominant in their life (this can be around race, ethnicity, religion, etc.) as well as where they grew up, as opposed to where their ancestors are from.
NOTE: Reviewed/Edited background material has only been brought over through here so far
Additionally, the definition of populations may also differ in scale. As mentioned earlier, ancestry can mean relationships across a couple of generations or tens of thousands of years. The 1000 Genome Project was an international research effort that aimed to create the most detailed reference of human genetic variation available at that time. Populations and superpopulations used by the 1000 Genomes Project that are both examples of creating population-esque categorizations. Superpopulations combine populations together, creating fewer overall categories. These categorizations don’t have a single genetic or biological characteristic driving them, but rather are subjectively and arbitrarily defined groups. There are 26 ethnically or geographically defined groups in the 1000 Genomes Project. There are 5 superpopulations that are composite groups focusing on a broader continental definition - not based on an individual’s current location, but instead their genetic ancestry. Given the mixing of populations throughout time, there may not be a single clear categorization for an individual into one of these populations or superpopulations.

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
text:
Clustering
Let’s take a minute to dive deeper into what these K columns mean.
Consider that you have a bag of Halloween candy. Perhaps you want to figure out a way to divide that candy into groups so that you vary the kind of candy you eat until you are out of candy. There are actually many ways you could divide the candy by different features. For example, you could divide it based on if it contains chocolate or has a fruit flavor, or you could divide it by texture, if it is crunchy or chewy, or perhaps you want to share with your Aunt who only likes candy that isn’t too sweet or with your cousin who really likes sour candy. As you can see there are many ways in which we could group the candy.
In order to group people by ancestry, we can group them by their SNPs. As discussed SNP variants may have been introduced through mutation and then may have continued to persist in a specific population or may have largely disappeared because of migration patterns. For example, if a population of a small number of people migrated to an isolated geographical location, any rarer SNPs may become more numerous among later generations that are descendants from these original settlers (this is called the “founder’s effect”).
We can try to group people by evaluating which SNP variants co-occur or seem to distinguish different groups. Going back to our candy example, we might find that a cherry flavor often co-occurs with chewy textures. These two features could help us to group our candy. We may have some candy that has a cherry flavor that are not chewy, but the two features together may help to create the optimal number of groups that we are trying to achieve for our candy sharing and pacing problems. We can use math to help us identify a more optimal number of population groups based on our SNPs. Clustering algorithms help us to reduce the mathematical distances of individuals within our groups or in other words, find clusters that have more similar individuals, without the clusters overlapping too much. So the data that we have in this case study has been used to identify that 7 clusters generally distinguishes the individuals into groups quite well. Since humans are quite genetically similar, allowing for individuals to overlap across the clusters is helpful. Therefore, as we will see an individual could have a portion of its SNPs overlap more closely with more than one cluster.

title: Open Case Studies: The Biology of Ancestry
text:
Reinforcement Exercise
While we have created an admixture bar graph in the Data Visualization section of this case study that resembles the original plot from the commentary, there are a couple of differences. We want to create an admixture bar graph that more closely matches the original plot from the commentary.
To visualize our data in a way that more closely resembles the plot from the commentary, we will use ggplot to create the stacked bar graph from our data. This way, we’ll have more control over the aesthetics of the plot. However, for ggplot to work well with the data, we will first need to make it into a form called long form.









In the example above, each sample originally had a single row for its data with different columns having different k proportions. Rows summed to 1. However, looking at the same data transformed to be long form, each sample now has multiple rows with only one column having proportions, but the corresponding value in the “subcategory” column tells you which k proportion that is.
This long form will allow us to work with all of the k columns at once. To do so we will use a function called pivot_longer. We need to specify (1: cols) what columns to pivot, (2: values_to) what to name the new column where the values will go, and (3: names_to) what to name the column were the original column names will be used as values.

ancestry_long <- ancestry_props %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("k"), values_to = "prop", names_to = "which_k")

Let’s check our work with head again.

head(ancestry_long)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  pop    id              which_k    prop
  <fct>  <chr>           <chr>     <dbl>
1 Amhara EGAN00001044421 k1      0.00001
2 Amhara EGAN00001044421 k2      0.00001
3 Amhara EGAN00001044421 k3      0.363  
4 Amhara EGAN00001044421 k4      0.00001
5 Amhara EGAN00001044421 k5      0.00001
6 Amhara EGAN00001044421 k6      0.637  


Nice! Now we have all our k values in one column and another column indicating what k it came from.
Now we will use this to make a plot like the one in the paper. We will use the ggplot function of the ggplot2 package. This is a famous R package for making visualizations. First we need to specify our aesthetics with the aes function to indicate what data will be on what axis and how we might color or group our data. In our case we want id(which is the gene name) on the y axis, prop on the x axis, and we want to color by what k it came from (which_k).
We will create a bar plot so we need to specify that with the geom_bar function. We need to tell R to plot the raw values of y, and we can do that using the stat = "identity" argument. Otherwise, it would count the number of rows for unique values in x.

 ancestry_long %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k)))+
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") 








OK not bad! We have made a plot that kinda looks like what we are trying to recreate pretty fast. However, we can do better.

We have some white lines between our rows of data on the plot.
Our y-axis isn’t readable.
We have different colors than the original plot.

OK first let’s try to tackle those white lines. If we add an argument of width = 1 to our geom_bar() function, this will allow all the bars to touch each other with no space between them. In other words they will take up the full space (up to 1). We can see how this looks compared to a plot with a smaller width argument.
First let’s try a much smaller width of .1. Here we can see that this makes a large amount of gray or white space between all the groups.

ancestry_long %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = .1) 








Now we will use width of 1.

ancestry_long %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) 








Nice, that is looking more like the plot we are aiming for.
Ok now let’s try to tackle that y-axis - it is basically impossible to see what is happening right now. Let’s try filtering our data first to just one population to make sure we are seeing what we expect and then we will clean it up. We can use the filter() function to filter our data. We need to specify that we are looking for a specific string value such as “Amhara” for the rows of the pop column. Therefore we can use filter(pop == "Amhara"). We need a double equal sign to tell R that we need a value exactly equal to the string. A single equal sign is often used to indicate values for arguments like when we used width = 1. So when R needs to know about a condition of equality or that a value needs to equal something specific, we need use two equal signs.

ancestry_long %>% filter(pop == "Amhara" ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) 








We can see from this that the y-axis is the value for the id column. We would instead like to have a label for the population.
Let’s stick with filtering to just this one population so we can really see what is happening. Let’s remove the ID label and then we can add a label for the full population. To remove the current y-axis, we can use the theme() function and use the axis.text.y = element_blank() argument to remove the values. This is a bit of a more complicated function. It has some specific requirements for how it is used, but it can change the look of nearly every aspect of a plot. See the documentation for this function to learn more. Basically, it can take many different options as things to modify, such as axis.text.y, which indicates that we want to modify the text of the y-axis and element_blank() is used to remove it. We can also remove our legend for the clusters as we don’t have that in the plot we are trying to replicate. We can use legend.position = "none" for that. This may seem a bit tricky but programmers and scientists would look up what the documentation suggests to know how to do this.

ancestry_long %>% filter(pop == "Amhara") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none") 








We still seem to have tick marks so let’s get rid of those. We can use axis.ticks = element_blank() to do so, similar to how we removed the y-axis text.

ancestry_long %>% filter(pop == "Amhara") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none") 








Notice how it still says “id” on the left? This is the y-axis label. We can remove that by renaming it to nothing by adding ylab = "". Notice that there is nothing between the quotes here.

ancestry_long %>% filter(pop == "Amhara") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none") +
  ylab("")








Nice! We are getting there. Now let’s add the label for the population. This is a bit of an advanced method, but we can do so making something called a facet column using the facet_col function of the ggforce package. We need to specify what column we want to use to label. We know we want the pop column since we want to have our populations listed. We use a tilde or ~ to indicate what to use. Then we need to tell where we want this to be listed and to match the plot we are aiming for, we should use the left. We can use strip.position = "left" to do so (otherwise it will be at the top by default).

ancestry_long %>% filter(pop == "Amhara") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none") +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left")








Nice! This is really starting to look good. One final thing we could do is rotate the text so that it isn’t vertical to match the Nature Commentary figure. We could also get rid of the gray background. To do so we, we need to add a couple of arguments to the theme function. We can use the strip.text.y.left function to do this and we specify that we want the angle of the text to be zero using element_text(angle = 0). To remove the background we can use strip.background = element_blank() (like we did earlier with the y-axis text).

ancestry_long %>% filter(pop == "Amhara") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        strip.background = element_blank()) +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left")








OK now let’s see how that looks for all of the populations. To do so we need to remove our filter.

ancestry_long %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        strip.background = element_blank()) +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left",
            scales = "free_y")








Ok so this looks a bit odd because all of the populations have the same height even though some populations have more individuals than others. So we need to tell R that is ok for our y-axis populations to take up different amounts of space and to have different values for the y-axis. We can allow for this using scale = "free_y" to let the y axis vary and space = "free" in the facet_col function to show in a relative manner how many samples are in each population based on the height.

ancestry_long %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        strip.background = element_blank()) +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left",
            scales = "free_y",
            space = "free")








Now let’s take a look at the figure we are trying to replicate again.

Looks like the major thing left now is the color. We can adjust it and make it match by using something called hex codes. These are very specific codes for colors. We can use the scale_fill_manual() function to color each of our clusters with the colors used in the original plot. We already figured out what these were, but you can check them using websites like https://imagecolorpicker.com/ to identify the original color hex codes. We have also figured out which k matches which color by trying this out a bit, but here we add this to our plot code.

ancestry_long %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        strip.background = element_blank()) +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left",
            scales = "free_y",
            space = "free")+
  
  scale_fill_manual(breaks = c("k6", "k7", "k1", "k4", "k5", "k3", "k2"),
                    values = c("#2B284B", "#FFE6AD", "#30A9E1", "#056EB5", "#2BA06A", "#EC5D25", "#A41252"))








Finally, it looks like our clusters are in reverse order. We can fix that with the group argument of ggplot and group our plot by population.

ancestry_long %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k), 
             group = pop)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        strip.background = element_blank()) +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left",
            scales = "free_y",
            space = "free")+
  
  scale_fill_manual(breaks = c("k6", "k7", "k1", "k4", "k5", "k3", "k2"),
                    values = c("#2B284B", "#FFE6AD", "#30A9E1", "#056EB5", "#2BA06A", "#EC5D25", "#A41252"))










Use the output from Data Analysis section instead now.


We took this a step further to add the majority cluster column for the geographical regions that was shown in the original figure. Click here to learn how we did this.

One more thing that the original plot has that our plot doesn’t have is a bar on the far side for each population. This bar is showing which cluster represents the greatest amount of ancestry for that population group of individuals in the sample. We can use our results from the Data Analysis section of the case study to add this.
To do this we need to figure out what the top k cluster is for each population and region.
First let’s save our original plot to an object so we can refer to it and add our new plot to it. Let’s call it plot1.

plot1 <- ancestry_long %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=id,
             x=prop,
             fill = factor(which_k),
             group = pop)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
        strip.background = element_blank()) +
  ylab("") +
  facet_col(~pop, 
             strip.position = "left",
            scales = "free_y",
            space = "free")+
  
  scale_fill_manual(breaks = c("k6", "k7", "k1", "k4", "k5", "k3", "k2"),
                    values = c("#2B284B", "#FFE6AD", "#30A9E1", "#056EB5", "#2BA06A", "#EC5D25", "#A41252"))

plot1








We already found the top k for each population earlier in the Data Analysis section, storing that in the avg_props variable / data frame and the max_k_for_pop column.
Now, let’s plot this, specifically we just want to have a color bar for each population, but to make sure we’re sizing it properly, we should join the avg_props data frame to the ancestry_long data frame. Otherwise the facet panel sizes won’t align well. However, we don’t need all of the columns from avg_props. We really just want the max_k_for_pop and pop columns.

to_plot2 <- full_join(ancestry_long, 
                      avg_props %>% 
                        select(pop, max_k_for_pop),
                      by = "pop"
                      )

To make this side plot, we will use a similar method as before, we want the same colors for example. Here we will fill this plot with the color that corresponds to the cluster that was typically the highest for the population.

plot2 <- to_plot2 %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = -1,
             y = row.names(.),
             fill = max_k_for_pop)) +
  geom_col(width=1) +
  facet_col(~pop,
            scales = "free_y",
            space = "free"
            ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text.x = element_blank()) +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("") +
  xlim(c(-1,0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(breaks = c("k6", "k7", "k1", "k4", "k5", "k3", "k2"),
                    values = c("#2B284B", "#FFE6AD", "#30A9E1", "#056EB5", "#2BA06A", "#EC5D25", "#A41252"))

Now let’s put our plots together. We can do so using the patchwork package. This allows us to combine plots with the plus sign. We can also specify how much width each should take up with the plot_layout() function.

plot1 + plot2 +
  plot_layout(widths = c(5,0.5), heights=c(12))







plot1

Glossary




Term
Definition


ancestry
An individual's personal understanding of their genomic heritage, genealogy, or family history. Often self-reported.


chromosome
DNA that is compactly stored by being wound around histone proteins. Found in the nucleus of the cell. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes.


codon
Stretch of 3 nucleotides in RNA that is "read" during translation -- each codon corresponding to a specific amino acid in the protein product


DNA
Double stranded helix ...


genes
Elements of DNA that are transcribed into RNA. They ...


genome
All of an individual's DNA


genomic variation
Differences in DNA sequences or the genomes when comparing individuals either within a population or across different populations.


mutation
Changes in the DNA (typically the sequence) that occur due to replication errors and exposure to mutagens (things or substances that cause mutations, such as UV sunlight)


nucleotides
The basic building blocks of DNA with 3 components: a nitrogen containing base - Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), or Thymine (T) + a five-carbon sugar + and a phosphate group


protein
Proteins are essential for all living organisms, performing important tasks in the cell. They are important for immune responses, structural support, information transmission, and powering movement. Proteins are complex molecules comprised of a chain of amino acids. The sequence and identity of amino acids impact how a protein folds into its 3D structure and there many different possible structures. Proteins are the result of translation (DNA --> RNA --> Protein).


RNA
Single stranded ... RNA is the result of transcription (DNA --> RNA)


transcription
The process by which RNA is produced from DNA.


translation
The process by which protein is produced from RNA.
